archetype.name: Rebuilding (unlucky in close games)
archetype.definition: A team that has climbed from last season's bottom-of-the-league play to merely below average, with a functional offense and a leaky pass defense, and a record that has lagged its play because the close games keep going the wrong way.

report.headline: Better than 2-8, still not good: a real offense undone by its pass defense
report.take:
The Jets are no longer the hopeless team of a year ago. In 2025 they finished 32nd in net EPA and 3-14. This season they sit 23rd, and the offense has climbed back to league average: 17th in EPA per play and 10th in success rate, with Geno Smith starting all ten games. That is roughly where the 2024 offense was. The defense has recovered from 30th to 24th in EPA allowed, but it is still the side holding the team down, which is an odd place to be for a staff in its second year that inherited a unit ranked 3rd as recently as 2023.

The record is worse than the play. The point differential implies 3.7 wins rather than two, Wins Over Expected sits at -1.7, and the Jets have won only 16.7% of their one-score games. Look at the losses to Green Bay by three, Miami by three and Las Vegas by five. Turnovers aren't the excuse either: the differential is +3 on the season. This team loses close games on third down and in the red zone. The defense is 23rd on third down and 22nd in red-zone touchdown rate, and the offense converts short-yardage runs at a 31st-ranked clip. Those are the plays that decide one-score games.

The pass defense is the core problem, and the numbers locate it precisely. It ranks 30th in pass EPA allowed and 31st against short passes, yet the tackling is fine (5th in missed tackle rate). So the issue is coverage that concedes easy completions, which lets offenses sustain drives without needing big plays. The run defense looks solid by season EPA (10th), but the recent box scores tell a less comfortable story: Buffalo ran for 201, Kansas City for 163, Miami for 156. On offense, the hidden tax is protection. A sack rate of 8.9% (26th) and 28 sacks allowed, alongside one of the longer times to throw, means Smith is holding the ball and absorbing drive-killers.

The last two blowouts came against Kansas City and Buffalo, two of the league's best, so the slide is not quite the collapse it looks like. The next three weeks are the softest stretch of the season: the Chargers, at Miami, and at Arizona, against opponents a combined 5-23. If Smith's ankle holds up, this is where the close-game luck should start to even out and a 2-8 team can play itself to something more respectable before Denver, Minnesota and Buffalo close the year.

strengths.title: A league-average, efficient offense
strengths.body: The offense moves the ball consistently: it is 10th in success rate and around 17th-20th in EPA, a big step up from the 29th-ranked unit of 2025. The passing game has carried it in good weeks, and the run game is serviceable at 4.11 yards a carry. This looks sustainable as long as Smith plays, because it is built on steady down-to-down gains rather than a handful of big plays.

strengths.title: Sure tackling and a sound run defense
strengths.body: The defense finishes plays: it ranks 5th in missed tackle rate and 10th in rush EPA allowed. That gives the unit a floor against run-heavy, limited offenses. The caveat is that the last month of box scores shows the run defense bending against better offenses.

strengths.title: Winning the turnover battle
strengths.body: Unlike most bad teams, the Jets don't beat themselves with giveaways. They are +3 in turnover differential, with only 9 turnovers in ten games. That removes one of the usual drivers of a losing record and suggests the close-game results are more noise than flaw.

concerns.title: Coverage that bleeds short completions
concerns.body: This is a real flaw, not bad luck. The Jets are 30th in pass EPA allowed and 31st against short passes, which points to soft underneath coverage rather than busted deep shots. It feeds directly into the poor third-down defense and drive-sustaining losses. With CB Jarvis Brownlee Jr. out, it is unlikely to fix itself this week.

concerns.title: Protection and short yardage
concerns.body: The line gives up sacks at a 26th-ranked rate, and the offense converts short-yardage runs at the 31st-ranked rate. The long time to throw suggests part of the sack problem is Smith holding the ball, but a 25th-ranked stuff rate says the line also loses at the point of attack. These are exactly the failures that turn one-score games into losses.

concerns.title: Losing the close ones
concerns.body: A 16.7% win rate in one-score games and -1.7 Wins Over Expected explain much of the gap between 2-8 and the 3.7 wins the differential implies. Some of this is the situational flaws above, but a lot of it is variance that tends to even out. Expect better close-game luck, not a different team.

trend.note: The offense peaked against Miami and Las Vegas in late October with its best passing days, then managed only 12 points in each of the last two games. Those came against Kansas City and Buffalo, so the drop says as much about the opponents as about the Jets. There hasn't been a win since early October, and the run defense has sprung leaks lately.

nextGame.headline: Worst offense in the league awaits, if Geno's ankle cooperates
nextGame.body:
On efficiency this is a mismatch in New York's favor. The Chargers rank 32nd in net EPA and 32nd in offensive EPA, with the league's worst run game by EPA. They still lean on the run more than any team, at 10.2 points under expected pass rate, which plays straight into the Jets' best defensive trait. Their line allows sacks at a 10.5% rate (31st), so a Jets front that had 8 sacks against Cleveland has a real opening. The Chargers' defense is middling (15th in EPA allowed) but generates little pressure: 13 sacks, 30th. That eases the Jets' biggest offensive problem. It is also the 30th-ranked unit against deep passes, while staying stingy underneath (10th on short throws) and on third down (7th). The Book still makes Los Angeles a 3-point home favorite, with the Jets at +130 and a low total of 40.5.

Availability is the swing. Geno Smith is questionable with an ankle injury, though Monday's tests showed nothing major. If he can't go, Cade Klubnik would start with one game of experience. Guard Dylan Parham (knee) and WR Omar Cooper Jr. (ankle) are also questionable, and CB Jarvis Brownlee Jr. is out, which thins an already weak pass defense. On the Chargers' side, Ladd McConkey, DT Justin Eboigbe and OT Trey Pipkins III were all inactive or on IR for their Monday night game against Baltimore. That also leaves them on a short turnaround. Their statuses for Sunday are worth checking, since a McConkey absence would further limit an offense that already struggles to pass.

waysToWin.title: Load the box, live off sacks
waysToWin.body: The Chargers want to run despite having the league's least efficient ground game, and the Jets are 10th in rush EPA allowed. Force them into passing downs behind a line with the 31st-ranked sack rate, and drives should die before the Jets' coverage weaknesses come into play.

waysToWin.title: Take shots over the top
waysToWin.body: Los Angeles is tough underneath but 30th against deep passes, and with only 13 sacks it rarely punishes a quarterback who holds the ball. That suits Smith's longer time to throw. Garrett Wilson and the WR2 spot (the Chargers allow the 28th-ranked PPR boost to WR2s) are the targets.

waysToWin.title: Lean on Braelon Allen
waysToWin.body: Lead backs have outscored their averages against the Chargers, who rank 29th by that measure. A steady dose of Allen keeps the offense on schedule and avoids the long third downs where this defense is strong.

waysToLose.title: Smith sits or plays hobbled
waysToLose.body: The offense has run entirely through Smith, and an ankle injury that limits him or forces Klubnik into the lineup would erase the Jets' main advantage. A less mobile Smith behind a line that already allows sacks at a 26th-ranked rate is a risk even if he plays.

waysToLose.title: Dinked to death on third down
waysToLose.body: Even a bad passing offense can live on short throws against the 31st-ranked short-pass defense, now without Brownlee. Meanwhile the Chargers' own defense is 7th on third down. If the Jets lose the third-down battle on both sides, a low-scoring game tilts to the home team.

waysToLose.title: Another coin flip lost
waysToLose.body: A 3-point spread with a 40.5 total points to a one-score finish, which is exactly where this team has failed. The Chargers' 12 takeaways (9th) give them a way to steal a short field, and a Jets offense that has stalled in short yardage may settle for field goals.

nextGame.watch: Smith's mobility on early downs: if he can hold up and attack the Chargers' 30th-ranked deep defense, the Jets should move the ball against a pass rush that rarely gets home.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense's efficiency looks real and should hold if Smith is healthy. The close-game record should drift toward neutral, because nothing in the turnover profile explains it. The pass defense is the structural problem and won't be fixed midseason. The schedule splits cleanly. The Chargers, Miami and Arizona are all bottom-tier teams the Jets match up with well. Denver, Minnesota and Buffalo are clearly better, though New England at home is a coin flip. A realistic finish is two or three more wins, which would land the team in the four-to-five-win range. That fits a team playing like a three-to-four-win club so far.

On the scoreboard, expect the offense to stay around 20 points a game, with the swings depending on the opponent's defense. The last two weeks showed what happens against the elite. Points allowed should ease somewhat in the soft three-game stretch before rising again against Denver and Buffalo.

confidence.note: Ten games of fairly stable efficiency, but QB health is uncertain and the recent results came against elite teams.
